Good news. You are on the shortlist, and they want to progress you to a panel next week.
Thank you. Could I ask how many people are still in the running?
Three. And one of them is internal, which I would rather you knew now than found out in the room.
That is useful. May I ask whether the hiring manager will be on the panel, or only the Group CFO?
Both, plus HR. Expect two competency questions and something close to a case study on working capital.
Then one more, and it is the one I always ask. Could I ask what the previous CFO found hardest there?
Nobody asks me that, and I will tell you. He never got the Brazilian numbers to arrive in the same week as the European ones. Two years, and he never fixed it.
Then I know what to ask them. I am curious what would have to be true, twelve months from now, for them to say this appointment had worked.
Could I ask how many people are still in the running?
May I ask whether the shared service center is already funded?

Let me tell you what happens after you leave the room, because candidates imagine something much more formal than it is. The panel has about eight minutes before the next person arrives. Somebody says a sentence, and that sentence usually decides it. He was solid but I could not tell you what he would actually do here. Or, she asked me three questions I could not answer, which is a compliment even though it does not sound like one. That is the whole debrief. Which is why the last five minutes matter more than people think. If you ask nothing, or if you ask about the process, you have given us no sentence to say about you. If you ask something that shows you have already been thinking about our problem, that becomes the sentence. And do not ask about the notice period or the package in a first meeting. Not because it is wrong to want to know, but because it will be the only thing anybody remembers.

I ask three questions at the end and they are always the same three, adapted. The first is about the number. I would be interested to know which figure this board looks at first when it opens the pack, because that tells me what they actually worry about, and it is never the number they say publicly. The second is about the last person. Could I ask what the previous CFO found hardest here, and it does not matter whether they answer honestly, because the pause before they answer tells me most of it. And the third is the one that has got me two roles. I ask what would have to be true, twelve months from now, for them to say the appointment had worked. Nobody prepares for that question, and watching a board try to answer it in front of you is the most useful five minutes of the whole process.

Claire tells Fernando he is on the shortlist and explains the format of the second round. Claire warns him that the panel will include a hiring manager he has not met. Fernando asks an indirect question about what the previous CFO found hardest. Claire says that is the question nobody asks and gives him a real answer. Fernando asks what would have to be true in twelve months for the appointment to have worked.
